short.title: Are You a WRDR Teacher?
short.text:
If you can predict what your class will look like two months from now, you might be a WRDR teacher: Wash. Rinse. Dry. Repeat.

I wrote about this in The Future Ready Challenge, and 20 years as a principal only made me more sure of it. If the lesson is boring to you, it's boring to them.

This week, take one risk. Try the weird lesson. Your students will remember it.

Need a fresh idea? I built a free tool that rebuilds an old lesson in a new style: askvic.ai (link in bio)

#teachersoftiktok #teachertok #teacherlife #teachersofinstagram #lessonplanning #edtech

linkedin.text:
"If you can predict what your class will look like two months from now, you might be a WRDR teacher."

I wrote that line years ago in The Future Ready Challenge. WRDR: Wash, Rinse, Dry, Repeat.

I still believe it. But after 20 years as an elementary principal, I also know why it happens. It's rarely a lack of creativity. It's a lack of time. When a teacher is planning at 9 PM on a Sunday, the lesson that already exists wins.

That's the problem I built VIC to solve. A teacher can upload a lesson they already have and ask for a new approach: inquiry, Socratic seminar, a project. VIC rebuilds it with the activities, a worksheet, an answer key, and an exit ticket. The teacher reviews and changes everything before it's used.

It's free for educators. If you lead a staff, I'd be grateful if you shared it with one teacher who's running on empty.

https://www.askvic.ai/

#Teachers #SchoolLeadership #AIinEducation #Principals

short.title: 5 Things Teachers Can Learn From the Band Room
short.text:
Before I was a principal, I was a high school band director. Picture 100 teenagers, each holding a noise maker, and your job is to make music. 🎺

That room taught me more about teaching than any class I ever took. Swipe for 5 lessons every teacher can steal from the band director.

Former band kids: which one did your director nail? 👇

#bandkid #banddirector #musiceducation #teachersofinstagram #teachertok #classroommanagement

linkedin.pdf_title: 5 Things Every Teacher Can Learn From the Band Room
linkedin.text:
As I talk with more and more school leaders, I've noticed something: a surprising number of us started out as band directors. I'm one of them.

I don't think that's an accident. The band room is one of the best teaching models in the building:

1. Classroom management, with 100 students holding noise makers
2. Project-based learning, because every concert is a real project for a real audience
3. Differentiation, with a first-year player beside a kid with years of private lessons
4. Communication, where a whole ensemble reads the language of a baton
5. Self-directed learning, because band kids practice when their section is counting on them

Full breakdown in the slides.

If you came up through music, I'd love to hear what the band room taught you about leading a school.

#SchoolLeadership #MusicEducation #Teaching #Principals

short.title: 2:07 AM. School Starts at 7:45.
short.text:
2:07 AM. School starts at 7:45.

When this student walks in tired, quiet, maybe snapping at someone, what do we see? Attitude? Or a kid who didn't sleep?

I built a free simulation that lets teachers walk one student's entire school day, and see how every adult response changes what happens next. It's made for staff meetings and PD.

Try it: drrobfurman.com (link in bio)

#teachersoftiktok #teachertok #empathy #urbaneducation #studentsfirst #traumainformed

linkedin.text:
It's 2:07 AM. A student is lying awake, listening to the noise downstairs, doing the math: up at 6:00, less than four hours of sleep.

At 7:45 that student walks into one of our schools.

What the adults see in the next ten minutes decides a lot. A tired kid, or a "defiant" one. A student who needs a minute, or a referral.

I built "A Day in the Life of an Urban Student" so educators can live that day from the inside. You make the student's choices, watch sleep, stress, and connection change hour by hour, and then reflect on the adult moments that could have changed the story.

It's free and works well as an opener for a faculty meeting or PD day. If you use it with your staff, I'd love to hear how the conversation went.

short.title: Grades Are Useless Symbols
short.text:
I wrote this in The Future Ready Challenge, and it still starts arguments. 😅

An A doesn't prove a child mastered something. Often it proves they figured out the test. Out in the real world, nobody hands you four answer choices.

Agree or disagree? Tell me why in the comments.

#teachersofinstagram #teachertok #grading #education #edchat

linkedin.text:
Years ago I wrote a sentence in The Future Ready Challenge that still gets me pushback:

"Grades are useless symbols from a less enlightened age."

Here's what I meant. An A tells us a student complied with an assessment. It doesn't tell us what that student can do with what they learned, or whether they'll still know it in June. In the real world, no one gets five answer choices.

I'm not arguing for no accountability. I'm arguing for better evidence: real use of a skill, explanation, projects, conversation.

What's one thing your report card can't tell a parent about their child?

#Assessment #SchoolLeadership #Grading #FutureReady

short.title: Principals: What Would You Do?
short.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

A teacher asks to move a student with big behavior needs to the other 3rd grade class. It might help her and her other 20 kids. But she can't explain how it helps him.

Approve it or say no? Comment your call. I put what I actually did in the first comment.

Want to practice decisions like this? Free principal simulation at drrobfurman.com (link in bio)

#principal #principallife #teachertok #teachersofinstagram #schoolleadership
short.first_comment: What I did: I didn't approve the move until we could name the educational, safety, or support reason it served. Moving him would give one teacher relief and hand the same problem to another class. So we kept him in place and built a behavior plan around the real need. It wasn't perfect overnight, but he, his teacher, and the class finished the year successfully. A classroom move should solve a problem, not relocate it.

linkedin.text:
In 2010 I built my first principal simulation, "A Day in the Life of a Principal," for graduate students in Duquesne University's educational administration program.

The idea was simple. You can't learn to lead a school from a textbook. You learn it in the moments: the parent in the lobby, the teacher at your door at 7:10, the fire drill during testing, the call you didn't see coming.

I've rebuilt that simulation from the ground up. You step into the principal's chair for a full day, make the calls on staff, students, families, and operations, and see what your choices reveal about how you lead under pressure.

It's free. If you prepare aspiring leaders, or you're one yourself, I'd love for you to try it and tell me what's missing.

https://www.drrobfurman.com/human-equation-suite/leadership-sim

scripts.script:
I've been an elementary principal for 20 years, and here's what I see every Sunday night: great teachers planning lessons at 9 PM. Not because they're disorganized. Because there's no time during the day.

[pause]

So I built something. It's called VIC. You give it your grade, your standards, and the kids in your room, and it drafts the whole lesson: the activities, a worksheet, an answer key, even an exit ticket. Then you change whatever you want. You're still the teacher.

It's free for teachers. Link's in my bio. Try it on one lesson this week, and tell me if it gave you your Sunday back.

scripts.title: Band director to principal (45 seconds)
scripts.use: TikTok / Reels. Bonus if you can film with an instrument behind you.
scripts.script:
Fun fact: before I was a principal, I was a high school band director. And honestly? That band room taught me more about running a school than my doctorate did.

Think about it. A hundred teenagers. Every one of them holding a noise maker. And your job is to turn that into music.

You learn real fast that kids rise to a real audience, that the strong players can lift up the new ones, and that nobody practices for a grade. They practice because their section is counting on them.

Former band kids, tell me in the comments: what did your director get right?
